paragraphs.original: \item Does knowledge distillation from a fine-tuned teacher model into a nano-scale student model yield higher detection accuracy than fine-tuning the same student directly on the wildlife dataset, given the domain shift from COCO-style classes to $225$ mammal species?

\item Which synthetic-image generator produces the most useful training data for this domain, and do the two criteria available before any detector is trained, apparent visual realism and per-image price, predict that ranking?

\item How does the composition of a class's training data, from synthetic images alone through a large pool of real photographs, affect detection accuracy, and does accuracy measured on the mixed test set hold up on the real test set alone?

\item How far is a nano-scale detector from real-time inference without quantization or any other compression step, and how much latency and model size does it save against the two-stage ensembles, measured on a target-adjacent proxy device?

Direct fine-tuning is the better recipe for this student. The directly trained model is clearly more accurate than the distilled one on every test domain, at every granularity, and in every band (\Cref{tab:kd-vs-direct}). The gap is widest in Band A, where the training images are synthetic and few, and where the teacher's soft targets were expected to help the most. The teacher's class distribution therefore added nothing that the labels did not already contain. Where it deviated from the labels, it seems to have done harm. \Cref{sec:limitations} explains why this form of distillation could contribute so little. Only one distillation configuration and one teacher-student pairing were tested, and the two runs differed in batch size (\Cref{sec:results_kd_basic_comparison}). The result rules out a benefit from this configuration. It does not rule out knowledge distillation for this domain.

paragraphs.original: The most useful training images came from a proprietary API service at its cheapest quality tier, prompted with the full, unabridged description (\Cref{tab:generator-ranking}). Neither of the two criteria that can be judged before training predicted this. The generator chosen for the production dataset because its images looked the most realistic ranks in the upper middle of the field, clearly behind the leader under the same prompt. Price did not predict usefulness either. In no vendor family was the cheaper tier worse than the expensive one. What does predict the outcome is how much detail the generator receives. Shortening the prompt roughly halved the downstream accuracy of both models tested, a larger effect than most differences between generators (\Cref{tab:prompt-length-ablation}). Earlier work found the same. Bare class-name prompts yield poor training data, and alignment with the target classes matters more than visual fidelity \cite{aziziSyntheticDataDiffusion2023}. The ranking holds for the data-rich classes only. On the rare classes, every generator scores close to zero, so this evaluation cannot rank generators for the classes that motivated generating images in the first place (\Cref{sec:results_per_class_structure}).

paragraphs.original: Half of a small real training set can be replaced by generated images, but not all of it. At the same training budget, a class trained on half real and half generated images is as accurate as a class trained on real images only, for two of the three models. The third model loses slightly (\Cref{tab:band-grid-real}). A class trained on generated images alone reaches only about half the accuracy of a class trained on real photographs. This matches the earlier finding that a classifier trained on generated images alone needs several times as many of them to match real images \cite{heSyntheticDataGenerative2023}. Both comparisons rest on single runs, and the bands contain different species, so the results are directional. The generator comparison, which was designed independently, reaches the same boundary. It can rank generators for classes with real photographs, but not for classes without them (\Cref{sec:results_band_granularity}). Generated images extend a small real pool. They do not replace one.

paragraphs.original: Accuracy measured on the mixed test set does not hold up on real photographs. Every model scores higher on the mixed set, and almost every class scores higher on its synthetic test images than on its real ones (\Cref{tab:domain-shift-delta}). Part of this is difficulty rather than domain shift, because a synthetic test image contains one centered animal and a real photograph often contains several. The rest is largest where the training images were synthetic. Both test domains rank the models the same way, so the conclusions of this chapter hold on the real photographs alone.

paragraphs.original: The band grid also shows where the remaining accuracy is lost. The detectors find almost every animal. They lose accuracy when naming the species, and most of these errors fall between the look-alike groups rather than inside them (\Cref{tab:granularity-gaps}). Within the groups, confusion is common but concentrated in a few pairs, and it mostly runs in one direction. The Asian elephant, for example, is usually labeled as an African elephant and rarely the other way around (\Cref{sec:results_lookalike_confusion}). A nano-scale detector loses its accuracy on this taxonomy by naming the species, not by finding the animal. A detector that could fall back to a coarser name would keep much of what is lost (\Cref{sec:further_work}).

paragraphs.section: Question $4$: Latency and Model Size Without Compression
paragraphs.original: Without any compression, the nano-scale detector needs under half a second per frame on the proxy CPU, about half the time of \textit{YOLOv5s} (\Cref{tab:embedded-latency}). The two ensembles are one to two orders of magnitude slower. The teacher ensemble takes tens of seconds per frame, and the pairing of \textit{YOLOv5s} with the same classifier takes several seconds. The nano-scale detector has a small fraction of their parameters and loses only a small part of the teacher's accuracy, which is itself an upper bound (\Cref{sec:results_embedded_benchmark}). These figures were measured at full precision and bound the latency from above. The accelerated integer path of the target remains unmeasured. The measurement confirms the argument of \Cref{sec:lit_md_speciesnet}. A two-stage ensemble of this size does not fit a mobile system-on-chip, and a single detector trained on the full taxonomy is two orders of magnitude smaller and faster at a small loss of accuracy.

paragraphs.section: Question $4$: Latency and Model Size Without Compression
paragraphs.original: The size of that gain, and where it came from, were both unexpected. \textit{YOLO26n} is the smallest, the most accurate, and the fastest detector measured. It is much smaller than \textit{YOLOv5s} and clearly more accurate, although both were trained on the same data with the same schedule. Two generations of progress within the same model family outweighed anything that tuning the older architecture could plausibly have returned. The same pattern is visible across the field at present, with large language models as the most visible case. Adopting the latest iteration often yields more than investing the same effort in the previous one. This is a general observation, not a measured result of this work. The measured part, a newer nano-scale model beating a larger and older one on every axis, is the strongest reason to repeat such comparisons whenever a new generation appears.

paragraphs.original: There is no comparable body of published results for fine-grained detection of $225$ mammal species in handheld photographs, and there is no benchmark against which the figures here could be compared. Whether the findings generalize beyond this dataset is a question this work leaves open.

paragraphs.original: Every model here started from pretrained weights, the students from COCO and the teacher from a large camera-trap corpus. Each of the nine COCO animal categories that map onto this taxonomy, from domestic cat to giraffe, has a counterpart in Band D (\Cref{tab:appendix-class-band-assignment-d}). Other well-photographed Band D species may also appear in those pretraining corpora, which are not fully documented. Part of the gap between Band D and the other bands could therefore come from pretraining rather than from the training composition. The COCO overlap is a quantifiable indication of that possibility. The question is not established here.

paragraphs.original: The distillation tested here transfers only the teacher's final class distribution, which is the least informative form surveyed in \Cref{sec:lit_knowledge_distillation}. A confident teacher's distribution is close to a one-hot label. Two properties of this setting weaken it further. First, the ground-truth species labels were produced by the same classifier pipeline that later became the teacher (\Cref{sec:speciesnet_matching,sec:teacher_finetuning}). The soft targets therefore largely repeat the hard labels, and they deviate from them mostly where the teacher is wrong. Second, a species label has one correct answer per animal. In domains where a prediction has no single correct outcome, such as predicting the behavior of other road users while driving, a teacher's distribution over plausible outcomes carries information that a hard label cannot. A strong teacher can be expected to help a student much more in such domains than in this one. Only one configuration and one pairing were run, so a stronger form of distillation on this task remains untested.

paragraphs.original: Two detector architectures were trained, and the starting situation chose both. The detector already in use fixed the family, and its smallest current member became the student (\Cref{sec:model_selection}). Nano-scale detectors outside that family were set aside for lack of time, so neither student won a benchmarked comparison, and no hyperparameter search was run on either. A broader set of architectures and a tuning study would likely improve both the accuracy and the deployment side of the results. They would also show how size and accuracy relate at this scale, which two data points cannot.

paragraphs.original: This work asked how a detector small enough for embedded hardware should be trained to recognize $225$ mammal species when real photographs are scarce for many of them. An automatically curated corpus of openly licensed photographs was assembled. Twelve generator and prompt-regime cells were compared on the same classes. Four detectors were trained and evaluated on real and generated test images. The runtime of each detector was measured on a device adjacent to the target.

paragraphs.original: Generated images can replace half of a small real training set without measurable loss. A class trained on generated images alone, however, reaches only about half the accuracy of a class trained on real photographs. Synthetic data therefore extends a small real pool and does not replace one. The amount of detail given to a generator matters more than which generator is chosen, and neither apparent realism nor price predicts the usefulness of its output. A current nano-scale detector trained directly on the data is smaller, more accurate, and faster than the larger detector of the previous generation. Distilling a far larger fine-tuned model into it does not improve on direct training. It loses its accuracy in naming the species once the animal is found.

paragraphs.original: The contribution is a measured map of where generated imagery helps a fine-grained wildlife detector, and evidence that a nano-scale single-stage detector resolves a $225$-species taxonomy at a fraction of the size and time of the two-stage ensemble it was compared against. Generators and detectors are improving at a pace that may overtake these findings within a few years, so the value of this work lies as much in a protocol that can be rerun as in the numbers it reports today.
